Why lower than the charger says?

WattFlow measures battery-side power — what actually enters the battery. Chargers display their own output. In between: conversion losses (~10% wired, 30–40% wireless) and the power your screen and system consume while charging. Phones also only draw what their charging protocol negotiates at the current battery level, no matter how powerful the charger is.
Peak In/Out here vs. the widget

These peaks reset every time you unplug, plug back in, or switch source (e.g. wired to wireless) — they cover only the current streak. The home screen widget shows a separate \"Today\'s Peaks\" figure that covers the whole day instead.

Battery alerts are delivered as a notification when your charge or low-battery threshold is crossed — Android requires notification permission for this. Unlike background recording, alerts have no fallback: without the permission, they won\'t appear at all.
Battery at %1$d%% — unplug to protect battery life

Lithium batteries age fastest at the extremes. Staying roughly between 20% and 80% reduces voltage stress and heat — the two main causes of permanent capacity loss. An occasional full charge is fine (it helps the gauge calibrate), but sitting at 100% or draining to 0% every day measurably shortens battery lifespan. That\'s why WattFlow defaults to alerts at 80% and 20%.

Screen-off power saving briefly pauses sampling. By default, WattFlow merges same-direction sessions separated by gaps under 5 minutes — closer to how you think about one charge or one drain. Turn this on to see every raw segment exactly as sampled, split at every gap over 60 seconds.

Exempts WattFlow from battery optimization so background sampling is not paused while the screen is off. Recording becomes more complete, at the cost of slightly higher standby drain (~0.5-1% per hour). On MIUI/HyperOS and similar systems you may also need to allow autostart in system settings.
WattFlow works fine without this permission — screen-off periods may briefly lack samples, shown as separate segments in raw mode.

Separate from battery optimization above: some phone makers (Xiaomi/HyperOS, Huawei, Oppo, vivo, and similar) add their own autostart block that can still stop background recording even after you\'ve exempted WattFlow from battery optimization. There\'s no way for WattFlow to check whether this is already granted — if recording keeps gaps overnight despite both being on, open this and allow autostart.
Open your phone\'s Settings app, find WattFlow under Apps, and look for an "Autostart" or "Auto-launch" permission to enable.

Common charging questions, answered with real test data
Charging power vs. battery % — real-world comparison
WattFlow battery-side readings (averaged per 1% level), from real charging test logs, devices anonymized
Dashed = charger/pad output (estimated from measured efficiency)

Dashed lines aren\'t measured point-by-point — they\'re the solid line divided by an average efficiency ratio spot-checked with a USB power meter during testing. Gaps in device B/C\'s lines are sampling breaks from swapping chargers mid-test; device A\'s wireless curve spans both screen-on (~7-16%) and screen-off segments with different efficiency ratios. All wired tests used the same original 120W-max charger and matching cable; the wireless test used an original 55W-max wireless pad, itself powered by that same charger and cable.
Tap to see the full chart
Why doesn\'t the charger\'s rated wattage match what the app shows?

The charger\'s rating is the maximum power it can supply; the app shows the power the battery actually receives. In between: cable resistance and the phone\'s internal voltage conversion (charger voltage is usually much higher than the battery\'s own voltage, so it needs stepping down, and that conversion itself loses some power). This gap is normally around 10-20%, which is expected.
Why does fast charging only hit top speed at low battery, then slow down as it fills up?

Lithium batteries charge in two stages: an early \"constant current\" stage at full current (highest power), then a \"constant voltage\" stage near full where current is deliberately narrowed to protect the battery, dropping power along with it. So the rated wattage is usually only reachable in a narrow low-battery window, not the whole way through.
Why does charging speed change a lot when you just swap the cable, same charger?

Cables differ in internal wire gauge and whether they carry an E-marker chip — a cheap cable may not even complete the basic fast-charge handshake, capping speed at a low tier regardless of the charger. Swapping just the cable can change the grade or wattage significantly with the identical charger, which is why Charging Benchmark records charger and cable separately.
Does a higher-wattage charger always charge faster?

Not necessarily. The phone itself negotiates how much power it actually wants via the charging protocol; the charger\'s rating is only the ceiling it can supply — like turning a tap fully open when the pipe itself is narrow. Both 120W-rated phones we tested peaked at only 40-57W in practice; a higher-wattage charger won\'t let the phone exceed its own limit. A pricier, higher-wattage charger doesn\'t mean faster charging.
Why does switching to a \"generic\" or third-party charger sometimes cause a sharp drop, not just a slightly slower speed?

Many phones use their manufacturer\'s own fast-charge protocol, and only the matching original charger reaches full speed. With a generic PD/QC charger, the phone and charger can\'t agree on the proprietary protocol and fall back to a more basic, noticeably slower universal tier — not a gradual slowdown. This is why swapping chargers sometimes looks like a cliff-edge drop rather than a gentle one. In our own testing, one charger only negotiated a ~27W PD tier, well below the 40W+ the other two chargers reached.
Is there really a big difference between the original charger and third-party chargers?

Not necessarily. We tested 3 chargers (2 of them original) on one 120W-rated phone, and all three landed on the exact same wattage ceiling — meaning the bottleneck at the time was the phone itself (e.g. its battery condition), not the charger. In other words, don\'t blame the charger the moment speed stalls.
Why do \"120W-rated\" fast-charge phones peak far below 120W in practice?

We measured two 120W-rated phones and even with their original chargers, real peaks only reached 40-57W, and only briefly at low battery — far below that number most of the time. The rated wattage is a theoretical ceiling, not a sustained rate; this gap is common on fast-charge phones.
Why does the same charger charge a phone slower and slower as the battery ages?

An aging battery\'s internal resistance rises, and the phone\'s battery-management chip (BMS) deliberately lowers the max current it allows through, to avoid overheating or accelerating damage on a degraded cell. This is battery self-protection, not an app or charger problem — check Battery Health Trend in Reports; if the full-charge capacity is well below the battery\'s rated capacity, that alone largely explains slower charging.
Why does the app still show a few watts of charging power after the phone reaches 100%?

Past 100%, the battery-management chip usually runs a short trickle top-off to offset natural self-discharge, at very low current that keeps decaying toward zero. This varies a lot by phone — some drop to zero current the instant they hit 100%, others keep tapering for a minute or two. Both are normal.
Why does overnight charging seem to speed up and slow down, even pausing for a long stretch mid-night?

Many phones (especially newer ones) have an adaptive or optimized charging feature: when it detects an overnight charge, it slows or pauses around 70-80% and estimates your wake time, then rushes to finish by then — reducing how long the battery sits at 100% to extend its lifespan. Seeing progress stall overnight is most likely this feature at work, not an app error or a fault.
Why is the loss on wireless charging so much bigger than wired?

A USB power meter reads the power flowing into the wireless pad, not what the pad actually delivers to the phone — you can't clip a meter onto a magnetic field. So the comparison is really power into the pad vs. power the phone's battery actually receives, spanning a much longer chain: DC-to-AC inversion, coil coupling, rectification on the phone side, then charge management — several more conversion stages than wired. On wired, the meter sits right between the charger and the phone, close to the battery, with only cable resistance and one internal conversion in between, so the gap stays small (~10-20%).

Wireless typically shows a much bigger gap (30-45% or more), and it fluctuates noticeably with coil alignment, power level, and thermal state — most of that loss becomes heat in the pad and the phone's back.

Real measurement (a 50W-wireless-rated test phone, one full 7%→100% run): with the screen on, the gap ran roughly 37-42% (ratio ~0.58-0.63); with the screen off, it tightened to roughly 28-34% (ratio ~0.66-0.72). That ~6-point difference is more likely explained by the phone's own screen drawing power (backlights typically use 1-3W) out of the same incoming supply, rather than the wireless coupling's efficiency itself changing with screen state — the app only reads battery-side current, not total device power draw, so with the screen on, some of the pad's power gets used by the screen before it ever reaches the battery. The whole chain's real efficiency runs roughly 58-72% (28-42% loss), varying with screen state, alignment, and power level.
Why does an external USB power meter always read a bit higher than what the app shows?

The meter reads power at the charger/cable side; the app shows what the battery side actually receives — cable resistance and the phone\'s internal voltage conversion sit in between, and that loss is physically unavoidable. We\'ve measured this repeatedly across multiple phones and power levels, and the gap holds steady at 10-20% without blowing up as power rises — a simple sanity check for whether a reading is trustworthy: the gap should be a small proportion, not a multiple.\n\nThis gap is really two things added together: cable/conversion loss, plus the phone\'s own power draw (screen, processor, etc.) — the app only reads current on the battery side, not total device draw, so with the screen on or background tasks running, some power gets used by the phone itself before it ever reaches the battery, making the gap look bigger than pure conversion loss alone (this shows up more clearly on wireless charging — see the wireless question above).
How does WattFlow calculate wattage, and what limits its accuracy?

It reads the battery\'s voltage and current directly from Android (measured by the phone\'s own fuel-gauge hardware) and multiplies them. That means the accuracy ceiling is set by how good that hardware sensor is — it varies by phone and manufacturer, and the app doesn\'t and can\'t \"correct\" a systematic hardware error; it faithfully shows what it reads.
Why does the app show \"discharging\" when the phone is powering another device (reverse charging/OTG)?

Android itself has no dedicated reverse-charging status flag — only charging and discharging. So when a phone powers headphones or another phone, the system can only classify it as discharging, and the app shows that faithfully — the wattage itself is accurate, it\'s just using one of the only two direction labels the system has.
Draggable live-watts pill over other apps while background recording is on. Needs the display-over-apps permission — the only optional permission WattFlow ever asks for.

Measures this charging setup for 60 seconds and grades it. Charger and cable both matter — either one alone can bottleneck the other, so swapping just the cable can change the grade with the same charger. Some phones only reach their fastest charging speed with the screen off, so a lower grade here may reflect that limit rather than the setup itself. For comparable results: same battery level range, screen on, phone idle.
Plug in a charger to start.

WattFlow keeps your screen on for the 60 seconds so the test can run without interruption. Some phones only reach their fastest charging speed with the screen off, so this result may read lower than that peak — but it\'s comparable across setups, since every test runs under the same screen-on condition.
Measuring… %1$d s left. Keep the phone idle.
Grade marked X: charge level was already high, so charging naturally slows near full — this doesn\'t reflect the setup itself. Retest below ~90% for a reliable grade.
Grades are only comparable across setups tested at similar charge-level ranges — a setup graded A at 20–23% isn\'t necessarily better than one graded B at 80–90%.
